rv.q: "Paramour" might be a bit of a mess but the dare-devil acrobats — flying to the top of the proscenium or snatching a hat while leaping over a standing man — get so close to danger that they make you feel alive.
The result feels more like a compromise than a successful marriage.
The show is undeniably gorgeous to look at, but it's also an incoherent mess that can't decide what it wants to be.
The resulting show, I’m sorry to say, achieves the singular feat of being simultaneously frenetic and tedious.
Alas, only the circus acts soar, sometimes literally, as the show’s musical and film elements play, at best, dutiful and uninspired parts.
But no matter how many times the action spills out over the stage and into the auditorium, it’s not enough to draw you into the mess that is Paramour.
What Cirque cannot do, alas, is craft a decent Broadway musical.

If Paramour has all the elements of a traditional Broadway tuner – songs, dances, conversation, characters – they are jumbled together in so topsy-turvy a fashion as to achieve a perverse originality, a three-ring circus of artistic muddle, miscalculation and mayhem.
It still hasn’t figured New York out.
The $25 million “Paramour” goes heavy on the company’s signature stunt sequences to our relief, because there isn’t much to be extracted from the often eye-glazing book and score.
The visual spectacle and acrobatic prowess on display are undeniably impressive.

We’ve come for the visuals and while it’s doubtful that Paramour audiences will come away disappointed in that department, they may wonder why that annoying story kept stopping the action dead in its computer-assisted tracks.
For aficionados of really bad Broadway shows, “Paramour” features one of the most outlandishly awful big musical numbers ever.
The production is a bumpy, swerving ride.

Paramour” is a lame, harmless alternative for international tourists who want to see a Broadway show but would prefer something with the Cirque du Soleil imprimatur than a long-running hit like “Chicago,” “The Lion King” or “The Phantom of the Opera.
Carlsson's lyrics are an embarrassing display of false rhymes and miss-accented syllables.
No team of show doctors could cure this bafflingly bad show set in the Golden Age of Hollywood.
Cirque du Soleil's Paramour is crashing and burning on Broadway - and there's no point in calling the paramedics.
